articles.title: How SentinelOne Blocked APT29's CaptiveCrunch Campaign
articles.context: Run these steps as a scheduled threat hunt rather than as a detection rule
articles.full_text:
Once the corporate network stopped being defensible, the control had to move to the device, as SentinelOne® has long argued.

That move carried one assumption with it. Wherever the laptop sits, name resolution tells it the truth and the agent can reach its own cloud. Almost nothing in the stack checks either half.

In July 2026, Microsoft disclosed a campaign that breaks both and named it CaptiveCrunch. A captive portal is the sign-in page a public Wi-Fi network pushes in front of you before it lets you online. Hotels, airports, conference centres, the splash screen you click through without reading. That is where this campaign starts.

CaptiveCrunch is the work of APT29, the cyber-espionage arm of Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service. Microsoft tracks the group as Midnight Blizzard, and elsewhere it is Cozy Bear. Outside the industry it is best known for the SolarWinds compromise.

We saw the same operation from the endpoint, across multiple environments we protect in three regions. We also found the adversary answering from inside the victims' own networks, which no public account of the campaign describes.

The Adversary Was on the Victim's Own Network Segment

Public accounts of CaptiveCrunch describe compromised captive-portal infrastructure, but our telemetry shows something narrower. The DnsPoison indicator recorded LLMNR responses on UDP/5355 carrying the adversary's address on roughly a third of affected hosts.

The queries carried randomised canary hostnames. LLMNR is link-local multicast that does not traverse routers. Anything answering those queries had to be sitting on the victim's own broadcast domain.

A Responder-style spoofer was sitting on the shared network, and no DNS server anywhere in the chain was compromised.

The techniques in play:

T1557.001 (LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay)

T1557 (Adversary-in-the-Middle)

T1659 (Content Injection), for the fake updates served in response to connectivity checks

T1584.008 (Compromise Infrastructure: Network Devices), per public accounts, for the captive portal gateways

From the same layer-two segment as the laptop, the spoofer raced the legitimate resolver and won often enough to matter. Across affected hosts, clean and poisoned answers for the same domain interleaved seconds apart.

Success rates ranged from 5.6% to 84% depending on the network. The spoofer replayed the genuine CNAME chain and rewrote only the terminal A record.

Then Windows delivered the lure itself. To check whether a network needs a sign-in page, Windows fetches a known file over plain HTTP. If the reply is not what it expects, it assumes a captive portal and opens the default browser for sign-in. All of that is documented behaviour.

An adversary who rewrites the reply on-path gets the operating system to open the browser at their page. The lure needed no email and no link, but everything after that still needed a person at the keyboard.

The payload was a browser updater matched to the victim's own browser. Microsoft documented ClickFix-style lures for this campaign. In those, the victim is walked through running a command. We saw no such lure on our endpoints, where downloading the file and launching it was manual every time.

Nothing you own sits in the path on someone else's LAN, so the control has to live on the host.

Disable LLMNR. It is the best host control and also the bluntest. It takes away the protocol the adversary is answering on, which no detection rule can do. LLMNR's fallback is rarely load-bearing in a managed estate.

Why the Usual Controls Were Not In the Path

The attack runs on someone else's network, so your network controls are not involved. Your DNS filtering is not involved either, because the spoofer forges answers on the wire before trusted resolvers respond.

The browser renders the lure because Windows told it to. The chain has no email, link, attachment, or scripting host in it.

There is also almost no behaviour to detect, because everything dangerous about this payload happens after a process is created. Before that, nearly every step belongs to the operating system or the network. That is not the kind of behaviour a detection engine is built to catch.

The payload is CornFlake, a Go remote access trojan. CornFlake in turn deploys ChocoShell, a PowerShell infostealer that runs entirely in memory. Microsoft's analysis of the same payload itemises what each of them does.

CornFlake, on the host:

Surveillance: A raw-input keylogger, clipboard monitoring, on-demand screenshots, microphone and webcam capture, and USB monitoring.

Persistence: Service registration, Run keys, and scheduled tasks, with a watchdog to restore whatever a defender removes.

ChocoShell, deployed by CornFlake and resident only in memory:

Cookie theft: Live cookie extraction from browser process memory and a defeat for Chrome's App-Bound Encryption.

Token theft: Microsoft 365 and Entra ID tokens lifted from the Token Broker cache.

Evasion: It disables AMSI through .NET reflection and runs a timing-based check for sandboxes and virtual machines before collecting anything.

Escalation: It chains three UAC bypasses in fallback order through the SilentCleanup task, wsreset.exe, and sdclt.exe.

Until it runs, the file sits inert in Downloads.

Deciding Locally, On the File, Before it Runs

The adversary controlled the network the laptop sat on and had cut the agent's path to its cloud. That left the file, judged on the agent with nothing else in the loop.

The agent convicted every copy that landed, each before it could execute. That is one hundred percent of delivered payloads in one hundred percent of affected environments. We verified both figures twice against the telemetry. One endpoint ran an agent nearly a year out of date and reached the same verdict as current ones.

Then we tested for the things that would mean we were wrong. Every check came back empty:

No process creations from the Downloads folder on any affected host

No adversary-attributable persistence

No lateral movement

No post-incident C2 contact

No payload hashes remaining

What It Looked Like in the Console

The investigating analyst recorded his screen while walking the Storylines on the endpoint where the payload came closest to running.

Because the Storylines are scattered across the campaign, he worked in two views. One was the management console, and the other was the Threat Operations Center, which clusters the same events more legibly.

Storyline 1: Delivery, With the Poisoning Visible On One Screen

It opens with Windows launching Edge with the connectivity-check URL as its argument.

Scroll into the DNS events on that same Storyline and the race is sitting there in plain view. One request for a domain resolves to a legitimate address. Scroll down, same domain, and it resolves to the adversary's address.

The same name was answered both ways, minutes apart, on one machine. Only injection racing a real resolver produces that pattern. Later comes the download, a browser updater with a (5) suffix on its filename.

The suffix means the browser had already written four earlier copies to the same folder. Our analyst took that to mean someone kept going back for it and tried to run the last one.

Deep Visibility does not record mouse clicks. Manual launching is an inference from the filename and the process chain, and we are flagging it as one.

Storyline 2: A Token Request While the Login Domain Was Poisoned

A different Storyline shows connections out to the adversary's address. Follow the URL events and the timing lines up with the delivery window.

The request is a POST to the OAuth token endpoint. Open the DNS events on that same Storyline, and the Microsoft login domain is already resolving to the adversary's address.

We can confirm token requests were issued while the poisoning was active, to a login domain resolving to the adversary. We cannot confirm what happened to them. Endpoint telemetry records the intended destination of a request, not the outcome of the TLS handshake. That handshake content is not something we have or can obtain.

Across the campaign there were 49 such requests. On one endpoint they began roughly 24 hours before any payload arrived, on another ten minutes before. Roughly half of the affected endpoints saw poisoning and no payload at all. That is a reasonable sign the malware was never the sole objective.

Storyline 3: The Verdict

It starts with the launch attempt, from the same browser process that had carried the operation from the start.

Static AI caught the download attempts, and the agent quarantined the file. On the launch attempt, the console records the payload blocked before launch and quarantined in under 100 milliseconds. It names the engine and the detection type on that event.

Earlier in the same sequence, Static AI convicted a .crdownload, the partial file a browser writes mid-download. That file was not named .exe, was not complete, and carried a partial hash rather than the payload's finished one.

Static AI read its structure and reached a verdict while the file was still arriving. It needed no signature, finished artifact, or lookup. The later (5) suffix shows the downloads kept coming. Nothing that landed ever ran.

Hunting for the Pattern, and the Identity Question the Endpoint Cannot Answer

Every behavioural signal missed at least one confirmed victim. Only two signals fired on every affected endpoint: the adversary's address and the poisoned DNS answer. Both depend on one address the operator can rotate at will.

Run these steps as a scheduled threat hunt rather than as a detection rule. Most of the work is correlation that costs something to run.

Primary Hunt: One Address Answering for Unrelated Domain Owners

Count distinct registrable domains (eTLD+1) spanning unrelated vendor ecosystems that resolve to the same public address. In our test against roughly ten thousand IPs and domains from affected environments, two surfaced, and both were the adversary.

Take DNS resolution events across the hunt window, keeping the queried name and the answered address.

Drop answers in private and carrier-grade ranges.

Reduce each queried name to its registrable domain using the Public Suffix List.

Group by answered address and count distinct registrable domains.

Map each registrable domain to its owning organisation and count distinct owners per address.

Step five separates a CDN from the adversary. An address answering for many domains owned by one organisation is a CDN. An address answering for many unrelated owners is not anything legitimate.

Counting raw answers instead fires on 389 of 9,375 addresses at a threshold of five. Azure Front Door and Cisco Umbrella top that list, and this hunt must never alert on that traffic.

Azure Front Door answers for azure.com, office.com, live.com, and microsoft.com. The adversary's address answered for Adobe, Apple, Akamai, AnyDesk, BeyondTrust, Brother, Microsoft, and roughly 128 others.

This hunt surfaced nearly a third of the endpoints we confirmed. No alert had flagged any of them. It runs across whole accounts, so it reaches machines beyond the ones you have already been handed.

Supporting inputs, weaker alone and useful in combination:

An LLMNR response carrying a non-RFC1918 address. Expect travel noise, since some hotel and carrier networks hand out addressing outside RFC1918 that is odd but harmless.

wpad.[your domain] resolving to a non-RFC1918 address.

The connectivity-check URL in a browser command line, followed within sixty seconds by an executable or .crdownload in Downloads.

Failed _ldap._tcp SRV lookups for your own domain controllers in the same window, placing the machine outside your own network.

If your staff roam, review the identity side for any suspected exposure window. Look for sign-ins from unfamiliar infrastructure, anomalous token issuance, and unexpected device registrations. Check there for what happened to the token requests.

Why the File Verdict Held

The agent convicted every copy of the file, on current and year-old agents alike. It did so while the adversary answered DNS for our own cloud endpoints in two regions. The network was the adversary's, down to the answer the agent received when it tried to reach its own console.

Static AI ships inside the SentinelOne agent. It reads a file's structure and reaches a verdict on the endpoint, without a signature update or a cloud round-trip. The Singularity™ Platform is built that way on purpose, because an agent cut off from its cloud needs a verdict.

APT29 showed here that it can cut an agent off from its cloud. Test what renders a verdict on your endpoints when the network is hostile and your console is unreachable. If it requires a lookup, that is your gap.

articles.title: Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver: The Trust Gap Attackers Operate Inside
articles.context: Public threat research found a single GitHub PFX file holding more than a dozen expired certificates, drawn from the 2015 Hacking Team leak and Chinese forums
articles.full_text:
Bring your own vulnerable driver (BYOVD) is having a moment in endpoint security. Some of the buzz is earned. Some of it is overblown. This series unpacks both and shows the evidence for each. This piece weighs the trust gap the technique exploits against what the data actually shows.

A long-revoked certificate still loads a driver into the Windows kernel today. Help Net Security traced a 2026 intrusion to a decade-old forensic driver whose signing certificate had expired and been revoked years earlier. The kernel loaded it anyway.

The reason is structural, and it explains why the defensive target most teams chase is the wrong one. Defenders track bad drivers. We pull the LOLDrivers catalog, sync the default driver blocklist, and watch the list grow. The list is not where attackers compete. They compete over signing trust. A signature is the scarce thing. A driver is just the disposable wrapper around it.

Trust Is the Scarce Resource and Drivers are Disposable

Think about a stolen credit card. The number keeps clearing for hours or days in the gap before merchant blocklists sync. The thief does not need a new card. They need the window where the old one still works. Card networks did not win by perfecting the blocklist. They won by scoring the transaction itself in real time, regardless of whether the number was flagged yet.

Signed drivers run on the same broken model. The blocklist is the merchant blocklist. The signature is the card. Attackers live in the propagation gap, and that gap is wide.

The defensive move that follows is to stop chasing the card numbers and instrument the transaction. This is the reframe no competitor owns. Defend the trust anchor, because the list will always trail it. The anchor is the signing trust itself: revocation, signature metadata, and the slow death of cross-signed-driver trust. A list of bad drivers grows forever. The set of trust mechanisms that let those drivers load is small and addressable.

The web learned this lesson the hard way already. Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) soft-fail meant a browser that could not reach the revocation responder simply trusted the certificate anyway. The kernel driver model carries the same flaw in a harsher setting. There is no soft-fail to debate, because the kernel does not ask the question at all.

The Proof Is In the Certificates

The economics favor the attacker because trust concentrates. Public threat research found a single GitHub PFX file holding more than a dozen expired certificates, drawn from the 2015 Hacking Team leak and Chinese forums. That one file forged signatures on thousands of malicious drivers.

A small set of compromised keys signs an unbounded supply of drivers. A few stolen keys against thousands of drivers means the list defenders maintain can never catch up. Block a driver and the cost is one recompile. Edit unauthenticated bytes, the file hash changes, and the same key signs a new artifact. The blocklist entry you just earned is already stale, because the signing key did not move and the key is the asset. SentinelOne®'s latest Annual Threat Report documents loaders that reintroduce effectively the same payload under fresh hashes to outpace simple hash-based blocking.

The trust-pyramid framing from that research describes a real structure. At the base sit individual drivers, cheap and disposable. Above them sit the end-entity certificates that sign batches of drivers, and at the apex sit the cross-signed certificate authorities the kernel anchors to. An attacker who climbs one level multiplies their reach across everything below it, and defenders who fight at the base are fighting where the attacker has infinite supply.

The same research showed how attackers manufacture fresh trust on demand. Tools forge signature timestamps, exploiting the pre-July-29-2015 cross-signed certificate exception by backdating a signature so it appears to predate the cutoff. An expired or revoked certificate becomes a working signing key again. The forgery does not break the trust chain. It satisfies it.

The kernel makes this worse by refusing to check revocation. Windows loads drivers signed with revoked certificates even when a local revocation list is present, and the decade-old forensic driver case showed the same failure in 2026. The operating system's kernel-mode signing policy accepts end-entity certificates issued before July 29, 2015 if they chain to a cross-signed authority. The policy codifies the loophole rather than closing it.

The defensive consequence follows directly. Blocking expired and revoked certificate driver loads, paired with the blocklist, beats the blocklist alone. The blocklist enumerates known-bad files one at a time. Revocation enforcement attacks the reusable key behind all of them, scaling against the attacker instead of with them.

A certificate authority revokes a key when it learns the key is compromised, and in a working system every consumer checks the revocation list and refuses the key. A revoked certificate carries a clear instruction, do not trust anything this key signs, and the kernel loads the driver anyway. The attacker did not defeat the trust system. They used the part of it that was never enforced.

The Driver Persistence Half-Life

Now the data. Against the LOLDrivers catalog, roughly one-third of catalogued vulnerable driver samples are not covered by the default blocklist. The June 19, 2026 pull puts it at 36 percent. That is 782 of 2,190 samples, absent from the default list. About 22 percent, 479 samples, load even with Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity (HVCI) enabled.

Call this the Driver Persistence Half-Life, the signature data point of this argument.

Be honest about what that number is. The 36 and 22 percent figures are point estimates from a single computed pull against one blocklist version. The method is published and reproducible: parse the enforced HVCI SiPolicy and the official block rules against the LOLDrivers JSON, match by file hash, then by authenticode metadata, and pin both to a commit and a version.

The caveats matter. The denominator is the LOLDrivers catalog, not every driver that exists. "Not covered" means absent from the default block rules, not exploitable on a given host. Hash coverage is brittle, because an edit to unauthenticated bytes changes the hash without changing the abuse.

The corroboration is real, and it is fewer voices than it looks. The catalog's own coverage metrics report that many LOLDrivers entries sit off the default blocklist, and public threat research corroborates the cadence qualitatively, confirming that systems can be attacked with a driver not yet listed. Two open tools reproduce the check itself, Trail of Bits' HVCI-loldrivers-check and a community block-rules checker, but no genuinely independent second count of the exact figures exists yet.

The lag underneath the number is the real exposure. The default blocklist updates only periodically through Windows Update, roughly once or twice a year, and deliberately holds back some blocks to avoid breaking legitimate software. The minimum disclosure-to-block window is a calendar quarter, and the historical window has run to six months or more. Most of these vulnerable signed drivers are reachable without admin rights, so the exposure is wide and the door is low.

The on-device reality runs worse than the stated cadence. Public reporting documented a Windows 10 driver blocklist frozen at a December 2019 version until an October 2022 fix. That is a roughly three-year gap between the published cadence and what shipped on the machine. A defender reading the cadence would assume quarterly freshness. The endpoint disagreed for three years.

Per case, persistence runs to years. SentinelLABS disclosed Dell's dbutil_2_3.sys flaws in 2021, and the signed-but-vulnerable driver was still disabling security tooling in 2024. SentinelLABS noted that the driver's certificate had not been revoked, leaving it abusable long after disclosure.

The half-life metaphor is precise. The catalog grows faster than the blocklist can absorb it, so the gap widens rather than closes, a long, slow decay that the attacker schedules around.

The method is reproducible against your own fleet. Run the same hash and authenticode match against the drivers that actually load, and the result is a number that describes your real exposure, a measurement you can repeat each quarter. The durable claim stays the honest one: roughly one-third of catalogued vulnerable drivers are not blocked by default. The precise 36 and 22 percent belong to one computed pull, a snapshot with a published method attached.

Blocking Everything Breaks the Business

The obvious fix is to block every old driver. That fix is impractical, and the platform's own documentation says so plainly: the blocklist "isn't guaranteed to block every driver," and blocks are held back precisely to avoid breaking functionality.

Vulnerable drivers are dual-use. Public threat research catalogued how most abused drivers ship as legitimate software components first. The same signed driver that disables an EDR this week was a working hardware utility last week. The blocklist maintainer weighs one confirmed abuse against tens of thousands of working installs. The hold-back is a rational choice under that math, and the exact gap the attacker schedules into.

The reboot gap makes the DIY approach worse. Independent analysis of the blocklist notes that a driver the policy would block keeps running until the next reboot, so an in-progress kill chain survives the moment you activate the policy. The attack surface reduction (ASR) rule that blocks vulnerable signed drivers only stops a driver from being written to disk. It does not block one already present from loading. Defenders who think they have closed the gap have often only narrowed the entry path.

The platform is moving the trust anchor. A Windows security update in April 2026 removes default trust for cross-signed kernel drivers, directly targeting the loophole the timestamp-forgery and pre-2015 exceptions opened. This is the industry bending toward the right target, attacking the reusable signing key itself, which is the correct altitude.

It helps. It does not close the gap. The April change applies to default trust going forward, so the 36 percent that sit off the blocklist today are not retroactively addressed by changing tomorrow's trust rules. The half-life keeps running on the inventory that already exists.

A separate chokepoint also remains in play. Public threat research documented one EDR killer used by multiple ransomware gangs whose coordination point was a shared packer-as-a-service, with no shared driver tying them together. The packer became the chokepoint when the driver did not. That is the pattern to internalize. Each fix narrows one path and exposes the next. Tighten cross-signed trust and the attacker leans harder on forged timestamps. Close the timestamp loophole and they lean on the unsynced backlog. The trust model has many anchors, and the attacker only needs the cheapest one still standing.

This persistence is not an accident of the technique. It is the product of an industry on the other side. SentinelOne's latest Annual Threat Report describes the industrialization of the modern cyber breach, with mature automation accelerating intrusions at scale. A trust gap that one researcher could exploit becomes one that a tooled-up criminal market exploits at volume, which is why the half-life persists across so many drivers at once.

This piece builds on prior work. Independent security research argued that admin-to-kernel is not a serviced security boundary and that blocklists are largely performative. That critique is correct and it stands. The contribution here is a measured persistence half-life, the certificate-concentration evidence behind it, and a trust-anchor reframe detection engineers can act on.

Stop Chasing the List. Instrument the Failure.

The card networks made the stolen number unprofitable by scoring the transaction. Defenders should do the same with signed drivers. Watch the trust event, because the catalog entry arrives too late to matter.

That means instrumenting the load itself. Sysmon Event ID 6 logs every driver load with its hash, signer, signature, and signature status, and any non-Valid status warrants investigation. This telemetry is low-volume and high-value, which makes it cheap to monitor and hard to flood. The Splunk detection content keys on exactly this event, with an explicit note that the alert needs triage rather than blind firing.

Signature-status detection and first-seen anomaly detection catch what blocklist matching misses. Alert on any driver load whose signature status is not Valid, including untrusted root, explicit distrust, and bad or invalid signatures, and on any driver whose hash, signer, or version has never been seen on the host before. Both approaches key on the trust attribute, so the known-bad list never enters the decision and the alert fires whether or not anyone has catalogued the driver yet.

The CodeIntegrity Operational log confirms whether your blocklist policy actually applied. Event ID 3099 confirms the policy is loaded, a blocked load logs Event ID 3077, an audited load logs Event ID 3076, and Event ID 3089 carries the signature detail. Pairing the block events with the audit events proves which drivers the policy stopped, which turns coverage from an assumption into a measurement. Given the three-year staleness the frozen-blocklist case showed, that proof is not optional.

The behavioral chain is observable end to end. A service is created via sc.exe, logged as Sysmon Event ID 1, and a System Event 7045 fires for the service install. A driver loads under Event ID 6, then a device control call (IOCTL) drives termination against protected processes. Public threat research watched one such loop run a repeating, fixed-interval termination cycle in kernel mode, stepping past protected-process defenses (PPL), and recent killers also unregister EDR kernel callbacks as a distinct observable before terminating processes. Picus mapped the same sequence across cases. Each step is a tripwire on the trust event, and none of it depends on prior knowledge of the specific driver.

The order of the chain is what makes it durable. The driver name changes every campaign, but the structure does not. SentinelOne's latest Annual Threat Report makes the same point about the kernel: activity at that layer can blind user-space instrumentation and leave a manual disk scan an unreliable assurance of cleanliness. Detection keyed to that shape survives a recompile, and detection keyed to a hash does not.

The mental shift is the point. A driver list is a finite answer to an infinite problem, and the trust anchor is small, addressable, and already moving. SentinelLABS research has lived at that anchor for years. The team co-discovered the POORTRY and STONESTOP WHQL-signed toolkit that drove the security advisory ADV220005, and proposed Authenticode-metadata blocklisting before that was standard practice.

Defenders are not behind because the list is incomplete. They are behind because they were grading the wrong exam. Score the trust event, and the half-life stops being the attacker's advantage.

Why This Is the Work SentinelOne Exists To Do

Scoring the trust event instead of chasing the list is the whole argument, and it is the argument SentinelOne was built to win. The platform watches the load itself, the untrusted signature, the first-seen driver, and the masquerading kernel service, from a vantage designed to keep reporting when the kernel turns hostile. Purple AI® carries that telemetry forward. Its Agentic Investigation capability reasons over the trust event the moment it fires, builds the timeline, and renders a verdict in minutes and seconds rather than hours and days. The propagation gap the attacker lives inside narrows when the verdict arrives at machine speed.

A control you have not confirmed is running is a control you are only hoping for, and most teams cannot staff that verification around the clock. Wayfinder, SentinelOne's managed detection and response practice, holds the line when your own team is asleep, fusing human threat hunting with the platform's autonomous investigation and Google threat intelligence. That is the reason the company exists. The trust anchor is small and addressable, and the advantage goes to the defender who instruments it.

Next in this series: The practical hunts themselves, the four distinct techniques hiding inside the phrase EDR killer, and the telemetry that catches each one.

articles.full_text:
For five years, SentinelOne™’s ThreatOps has inspired a global defender movement. What began in 2020 as a threat hunting webinar has grown into an industrial-scale gamified platform that has trained over 19,000 blue teamers, influenced over $661 million in closed-won revenue (September 2023–September 2026), and spawned the Sentinels League Threat Hunting World Championship.

As we mark five years of ThreatOps innovation, defenders worldwide are gearing up for the ultimate showcase: the Sentinels League Grand Final, hosted live on stage at OneCon 2026 in Las Vegas from October 20–22, 2026.

The Evolution of ThreatOps

The origin of ThreatOps dates back to April 2020, when Solutions Engineer (SE) Director Ryan Merrick launched a two-hour threat hunting webinar covering MITRE ATT&CK concepts, indicators of compromise (IOCs), and the distinction between hunting and searching. While educational, the team recognized that defenders needed hands-on experience interacting with real product telemetry.

In May of 2020, SE Joseph Poyner sketched a vision in a team chat channel: standing up a Capture the Flag (CTF) game that would walk players through the product, requiring them to search deep visibility telemetry for malicious process connections to find hidden flags.

With the support and guidance of SE leaders Tommy Hui, Dave Gold, Keith Weisman, and Jared Phipps, the team secured a dedicated CTF line item in the FY21 budget, turning a side project into an official initiative. That initial sketch defined the exact game format ThreatOps still runs today. By August 2020, the team had stood up a dedicated console and created a parallel ransomware workshop track.

The first live game ran in October 2020 for SentinelOne's product management team, followed by the first customer workshop in EMEA. Rapid scaling and industrialization soon followed:

Public Challenges and Accreditation (2021): In March 2021, ThreatOps launched its first public challenge featuring cash prizes, expanding across named accounts, partner channels, and UK regional teams.

Industrialization & Platform (2022): PJ Norris built a game-creator program to train SEs globally while securing CPE accreditation. At the same time, Brian Martin created a platform to automate game provisioning, data replays, and self-service registration. This new platform reduced workshop setup times from two days to under five minutes.

Hackathon (2023) & Content Editor: In September 2023, the team met for the first ThreatOps Hackathon in Detroit, Michigan, where SEs spent a week building content, including the new Purple AI game (featuring GLaDOS). Shortly thereafter, Ryan O’Grady built a new game editor that streamlined the process for creating and publishing new game content.

Multi-Surface & AI Expansion (2024–2025): The program expanded into every surface SentinelOne ships, including a new SDL Deep Dive game, Cloud Security, the Need for Speed-themed Hyperautomation game featuring live API interactions, and the Data Pipelines games. These games were made possible by collaboration with SE champions, including John Pease and Marco Rottigni.

Through continuous craft and automation, ThreatOps transformed threat hunting from a manual class into an enterprise-grade operational standard.

Enterprise Protection and $661M+ Revenue

The impact of ThreatOps shows up in two places: the number of defenders it has trained and the revenue it has influenced.

Empowering 19,000+ Global Defenders

What started as an internal workshop has grown into a massive global educational engine. Between September 2023 to September 2026, ThreatOps has built and deployed 5,215 game instances across 9 unique game types, generating a total of 27,899 player seats and reaching 19,211 unique players across 5,869 email domains.

The program's core audience is overwhelmingly enterprise-focused, with 87.4% corporate participation representing over 16,700 unique corporate defenders. Practitioners from world-class organizations regularly refine their skills in ThreatOps competitions, including teams from Orange and Orange Cyberdefense, Exclusive Networks, Cloud4C, GoDaddy and many more. This global footprint is sustained by an active internal community of 407 game owners.

$661.8M+ Closed-Won Revenue Influence

Beyond skill development, interactive threat hunting has become one of SentinelOne's most potent catalysts for customer acquisition and technical evaluation. Our analysis reveals that ThreatOps engagements have influenced $661.8 million in closed-won revenue across 6,435 deals and 1,538 corporate accounts (Sept 2023–Sept 2026).
